title: TSMC Pledges $100 Billion More for Arizona as AI Demand Drives Record Profit
excerpt: The world's largest chipmaker raised its capital spending forecast and upgraded growth guidance after second-quarter profit surged 77%, reinforcing its bet on a multi-year AI boom.
body:
• TSMC pledged an additional $100 billion to expand its Arizona chipmaking facilities, bringing its total U.S. investment to $265 billion — the largest foreign direct investment in American history.
  • Second-quarter profit surged 77% to a record $22 billion, beating analyst estimates by a wide margin as AI chip demand accelerated.
  • The company raised its 2026 capital spending forecast to $60–64 billion, up from the previous $52–56 billion range, signalling confidence in sustained AI demand through 2030.
  • TSMC's first Arizona fab is operational and achieving yields "as good as" its flagship Taiwan facility, with three more fabs in various stages of construction.

A $265 Billion Bet on American Chipmaking

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. announced plans to invest an additional $100 billion in its Arizona operations, bringing total planned U.S. spending to $265 billion. The commitment, disclosed alongside blockbuster second-quarter results on Thursday, would fund four additional advanced semiconductor manufacturing facilities and expand TSMC's Arizona footprint to 12 leading-edge fabrication and packaging plants plus an R&D centre.

"We believe this investment will further foster the development of the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem, strengthen the supply chain, and support significant job creation," CEO C.C. Wei said in a statement. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick called it a move that "will create tens of thousands of American jobs."

Record Quarter Fuelled by AI Demand

The investment expansion was backed by TSMC's strongest quarter on record. Net income jumped 77% year-on-year to T$706.6 billion ($22 billion), comfortably beating the market forecast of T$632.6 billion. Revenue climbed 36% to T$1.27 trillion ($40.2 billion), with advanced technologies — chips at 7-nanometer and smaller nodes — accounting for 77% of total wafer revenue.

The company's 2-nanometer chips, still in their early ramp phase, contributed 3% of wafer revenue in the quarter, while 3-nanometer chips made up 30%. TSMC raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $60–64 billion, up from $52–56 billion, and upgraded its full-year revenue growth forecast from "over 30%" to "over 40%."

"Our customers and customers' customers, who are mainly the cloud service providers, continue to provide us with their very strong signal and positive outlook. Thus, our conviction in the multi-year AI megatrend remains very high."

— C.C. Wei, CEO, TSMC

Arizona Fabs: From Groundbreaking to Production

TSMC's first Arizona fab is now operational and achieving chip yields "as good as" the company's flagship facility in Taiwan, according to CFO Wendell Huang. The second fab will shortly begin equipment installation, a third is under construction, and preparatory work has started on a fourth along with the site's first advanced packaging facility.

The pace is not without obstacles. Huang acknowledged "physical constraints — the number of construction workers available, the infrastructures available" and said the company would work closely with the U.S. government to resolve them. TSMC also faces a potential $1 billion penalty to settle a U.S. export control investigation over a chip that ended up inside a Huawei AI processor.

What This Means for the Global Chip Supply Chain

TSMC's Arizona expansion fits into a broader geopolitical realignment of semiconductor manufacturing. President Trump has pushed aggressively for domestic chipmaking, saying the U.S. should control 50% of global capacity by the end of his term. TSMC's investment, combined with Intel's government-backed expansion and Samsung's planned U.S. facilities, is reshaping a supply chain long concentrated in East Asia.

For Indian IT services companies that serve semiconductor clients, the Arizona buildout creates consulting and staffing opportunities. Indian-origin engineers already form a significant portion of the U.S. semiconductor workforce, and the expansion of fab operations will intensify demand for talent in chip design, process engineering and manufacturing support.

Looking Ahead

Despite the bullish numbers, TSMC's Taipei-listed shares fell 7.3% on Friday as investors weighed rising capital expenditure against margin pressure. The stock remains up nearly 50% year-to-date. Huang struck a confident tone: "We do not intend to leave anything on the table. Our competitors are good, but we are even better."

The third quarter is expected to be driven by continued ramping of 2-nanometer technology, the sharpest indicator yet of whether AI chip demand can sustain the semiconductor industry's most aggressive capital cycle in decades.
